opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the opportunity is enormous, and it comes down to time. Most liver cancers are found late, when treatment options are limited. But many patients who develop liver cancer have been in the healthcare system for years. They have chronic liver disease, fatty liver, hepatitis, cirrhosis, and they're getting CT scans or MRIs along the way. The information is often already sitting in those images. We just haven't been able to read it.

A radiologist looks at a scan to answer a specific clinical question: is there a lesion, has something grown. But the human eye isn't built to pick up subtle changes in texture, tissue heterogeneity, or patterns across thousands of voxels that may signal the liver is moving toward malignancy. That's where quantitative imaging, radiomics, and deep learning come in. We can pull out features that aren't visible and look at how they change over time in the same patient.

If we can find those early signatures, we can do a few things. We can stratify risk, so that high-risk patients get closer surveillance and low-risk patients aren't over-tested. We can catch disease at a stage where surgery, ablation, or transplant is still possible. And we can learn more about the biology of how cancer develops in the liver, because the imaging becomes a window into the process.

There are real challenges. We need large, well-annotated, longitudinal datasets, models that hold up across scanners and institutions, and validation that shows we're actually changing outcomes for patients, not just producing a nice prediction. But the fact that we can get this from scans people are already having, without new invasive tests, is what makes it so compelling to me.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using imaging to identify liver cancer risk and guide surveillance, but it does not propose chemotherapy or immunotherapy to prevent liver metastases.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The opportunity, to me, is really about timing. Most liver cancers, and most liver metastases from colorectal cancer, which is where a lot of my work sits, are found when they're already large enough for a radiologist to point at. But the liver doesn't go from healthy to a tumor overnight. There's a whole stretch of time before that where the tissue is changing: the texture, the way it takes up contrast, subtle shifts in fat and fibrosis, the microenvironment getting ready to host a tumor. Those changes are in the CT and MRI scans we're already acquiring. We just haven't had tools sensitive enough to read them.

That's where imaging AI gets exciting. These models can pick up patterns in voxel-level data that a human eye isn't built to see, and they can do it quantitatively and reproducibly across thousands of patients. So instead of asking "is there a lesion here," we can start asking "does this liver look like one that's about to develop disease." If we can answer that, it changes the whole clinical conversation. You could move from surveillance every six or twelve months to risk-adapted monitoring. You could intervene earlier, with smaller resections or ablation, when outcomes are dramatically better. And for patients already treated for colorectal cancer, you could potentially flag who's likely to recur in the liver before it shows up.

I'll be honest that there's a lot of hard work between here and there. These models need to be validated across scanners, institutions, and populations, and we have to understand what they're actually keying on, not just that they perform well on a test set. But the raw signal is there in the images, and the clinical need is enormous. That combination is why I think this is one of the most promising places to be working right now.

r001.rationale: The response suggests risk-adapted monitoring and earlier local treatment such as resection or ablation, but does not propose chemotherapy or immunotherapy to prevent liver metastases in high-risk patients.

astra-6.text:
The opportunity is to look beyond whether there’s a tumor visible today and ask whether the liver is showing changes that could signal a higher risk of cancer in the future. AI could help us pick up subtle patterns in imaging that are difficult to recognize by eye.

If we can validate those patterns, we could use them to identify people who might benefit from closer surveillance and potentially detect cancer earlier, when there are more treatment options. The key is showing that those signals reliably predict risk and that acting on them actually improves care.

r001.rationale: The response proposes closer surveillance and earlier detection based on imaging risk signals. It does not propose chemotherapy or immunotherapy to prevent liver metastases.
